lit: Gulluoglu et al. (2026), the course paper, asks whether current AI tools can turn the molecule drawings in real journal PDFs into SMILES, a task that published benchmarks avoid by testing single, cleanly cropped images. The authors hand-curated an answer key for six open-access 2026 papers (222 drawn molecules; 220 unique structures after canonicalization, the count our scorer uses) and scored every system by exact match of canonical SMILES. Existing readers run on Docling's figure images found almost nothing (DECIMER and MolVec none, MolScribe one molecule), because they read plots, tables and text as molecules and cannot combine a scaffold with its R-group table. A Claude Code pipeline (Docling figures, a molecule gate, MolScribe, RDKit) found 13 molecules, and ChatGPT-5.5 output 5,329 SMILES to find 32. The authors conclude that figure segmentation, not recognition, is the bottleneck. Our results support that and show what comes next. With the same MolScribe reader, our pipeline on MolDetV2 crops found 54 molecules instead of 13, so better segmentation was the first gain. The molecules still missed are mostly scaffold-plus-R-group structures in papers 2, 4 and 19, which no reader can produce from a single crop.

Yan et al. (2026) address the problem that protein-ligand bioactivity data sit in papers as text, tables, and figures, and that using them requires exact ligand structures, including Markush structures whose R-groups are defined elsewhere on the page. BioMiner's structure agent detects molecules with MolDetV2, reads them with its own OCSR model MolGlyph, and uses a fine-tuned vision-language model to link labels and enumerate R-groups, which RDKit then joins onto the scaffold. The authors also release BioVista, a benchmark of 500 papers with 16,457 bioactivity entries and 8,735 structures. BioMiner reaches an F1 score of 0.32 on full bioactivity triplets, and MolGlyph scores 0.764 overall, 0.770 on Markush structures and 0.504 on chiral ones. Our MolGlyph run is close: 78.0% overall and 50.8% on chiral crops (Table 1). In our internal papers, BioMiner found only 73 of 220 molecules (Table 3), in line with the modest end-to-end scores the authors report, and its language-model step was the only change that helped the R-group tables.

Chen et al. (2024) address the problem that molecule images vary widely in drawing style, abbreviations, and stereochemistry. MolNexTR is an image-to-graph model: a ConvNeXt and vision-transformer encoder feeds a decoder that predicts atoms with their coordinates, and then the bonds, and rule-based steps then fix stereochemistry and expand abbreviations. The authors report 81% to 97% exact-match accuracy on their test sets, including 82.1% on JPO and 93.8% on USPTO, and note that R-group information held in text or tables is left for future work, which is the gap our pipeline targets. Our runs scored lower on all four older sets, by 14 points on CLEF, 5 on UOB, 15 on USPTO, and 29 on JPO (Table 2), and MolNexTR reached 43.4% on BioVista (Table 1), well below MolGlyph's 78.0%. Its USPTO lead over MolGlyph comes from stereochemistry (Adranly, 2026), consistent with its rule-based chirality step.

Rajan et al. (2023) address the problem that most published chemical structures exist only as images, and that no open tool combined finding, filtering and reading them. DECIMER.ai chains three parts: a Mask R-CNN that segments structures from page images, a classifier that separates chemical from non-chemical images, and the DECIMER Image Transformer, an EfficientNet-V2 encoder with a Transformer decoder that writes SMILES. The transformer was trained on more than 450 million synthetic depictions of PubChem molecules, including synthetic Markush structures. The authors report an average Tanimoto similarity above 0.95 on their own test sets and exact-match accuracy of 61% to 88% on JPO, CLEF, USPTO and UOB, but note that R-group labels are harder to read and that MolScribe beat DECIMER when both were trained on the same data. Our DECIMER 2.8.0 run shows a similar weakness on journal figures: it read 30.0% of BioVista crops, 54.5% of those without R-groups and none of the 3,596 Markush crops (17.0% once its R-group labels are rewritten as *), and 14.3% of its outputs were not valid SMILES (Table 1; Chhetri, 2026). We therefore do not use it as a reader in the pipeline.
